worksheets.title: How we see: thinking like Ibn al-Haytham

items.p: Many people feel they can tell when someone is staring at the back of their head. Plan a fair test to find out if this is true.
items.a: My sister sits with her back to me. For each of 20 turns, I toss a coin. Heads, I stare at her head. Tails, I look away. She says 'staring' or 'not staring' each time, and I write it down. I stay quiet so she gets no clues. Just guessing would get about 10 right. If she gets many more than 10, again and again, the feeling may be real.
items.why: A strong plan decides 'stare or not' by chance, removes sounds and other clues, repeats many times, and compares with what guessing alone would give. Careful tests like this have mostly found no effect. Eyes catch light, and send nothing out.

items.p: Selig Hecht and his team found that a person can notice a faint flash when only a few photons are caught. Photons are the tiniest bits of light. What does this tell us?
opts: The eye is extremely sensitive to light
The eye needs huge amounts of light
items.why: Catching only about 5 to 14 photons is close to the smallest amount of light there can be. So the eye is one of the most sensitive light detectors we know. Picking 'huge amounts' gets it backwards. Picking 'photons are big' is wrong, because photons are far too small to see one by one.

items.p: Scientists all agree that a person can notice a single photon.
items.why: False. Rod cells can respond to one photon. One 2016 study suggested a person can sometimes notice a single photon. Other scientists want it repeated before they agree.

items.p: In India, doctors in Project Prakash help children who were born blind with cloudy lenses. After an operation, their eyes work. But at first, many could not match a shape they had felt with their hands to the same shape seen with their eyes. What does this tell us about seeing?
items.a: Seeing is not only done by the eyes. The brain has to learn to make sense of the signals. Their eyes worked after the operation, but their brains still needed time to learn.
items.why: A strong answer separates the eye (which now works) from the brain (which must learn). Project Prakash is led by Pawan Sinha.

items.p: Why do photos taken with a flash sometimes show red eyes?
opts: The flash reflects off the back of the eye, which is full of blood vessels
items.why: The flash goes in through the wide-open pupil, reflects off the back of the eye, which is rich in blood, and comes straight back to the camera. Picking 'the eyes make red light' mixes up eyes and light sources. Picking 'the camera is broken' does not fit, because the same camera takes normal photos in daylight.

items.p: Why can't you see your own eyes without a mirror?
opts: Light from your eyes goes away from you, and nothing bounces it back
Your eyes are too close to see
items.why: To see something, light from it must reach your eyes. Light from the front of your eye goes away from you, out into the room. A mirror reflects it back to you. Picking 'too close' does not fit, because you can see your nose, which is just as close. Picking 'invisible' is wrong, because other people can see your eyes.

items.p: Light from a faint star travels a very long way and enters your eye. Explain, using the word 'photon', what happens when it reaches your retina.
items.a: A photon from the star comes in through my pupil and lands on a rod cell in my retina. It hits a tiny molecule and makes it change shape. That starts a signal that goes along the optic nerve to my brain.
items.why: A strong answer follows the photon all the way: pupil, retina, molecule, signal, optic nerve, brain. Every act of seeing starts with photons changing the shape of molecules in the retina.

items.p: Sort these statements about seeing.
items: We see when light enters our eyes.
Rod cells work best in dim light.
The brain fills in the blind spot.
Whether the red you see looks the same as the red your friend sees.
What a bee experiences when she looks at a flower.
Whether we see the world as it really is.
items.a: see items
items.why: The path of light, the rod cells and the blind spot have all been tested many times. What seeing feels like from the inside, for you, a friend or a bee, is still an open question. Scientists can measure the signals, but not yet the experience.

items.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 5, sits on a dark terrace for 20 minutes and can now see many stars. Then a neighbour's bright white torch shines in her eyes for a moment. What happens next?
opts: She sees fewer stars, and has to wait again for her eyes to get used to the dark
She sees more stars, because the torch added light
items.why: In the 20 minutes, her rod cells slowly built up their light-catching chemical. A flash of bright light uses it up in a moment. Picking 'more stars' forgets that the torch lights her eyes, not the stars. This is why star watchers use only dim red torches.

items.p: In the blind spot activity, the dot vanished when the card was about 25 cm from your eye. What happens if you move the card back to 50 cm, still staring at the cross?
opts: The dot comes back, because its light no longer lands on the blind spot
The dot stays hidden at every distance
items.why: The dot only vanishes when its light lands exactly on the blind spot. At other distances it lands on cells that can catch light, so you see it again. Picking 'hidden at every distance' treats the dot as gone, when only its light's landing place changed.

items.p: In the story The Lamp-Seller's Daughter, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, who lived in Cairo, makes a small hole in the shutter of a dark room. A donkey stands outside in the sunlight. Draw the room, the hole and the donkey. Draw arrows to show how the picture of the donkey got onto the wall.
items.a: An arrow from the Sun to the donkey, then arrows from the donkey, through the hole, to the wall.
items.why: Light from the Sun bounced off the donkey. Some of it came through the hole and landed on the wall. A strong drawing has every arrow pointing away from the Sun and towards the wall.
items.art: An outline of a dark room with a small hole, and a donkey in a sunny street outside.

items.p: Light bounces off everything in a room. So why isn't a white wall covered in pictures of everything, all mixed up?
items.a: Light from every point of every thing spreads out in all directions, and it all mixes on the wall. So the wall just looks bright. A small hole, or the pupil and lens of an eye, lets in light from each point in only one direction. So each point lands in one place, and that makes a picture.
items.why: This is the puzzle Ibn al-Haytham worked on. A strong answer says the light is mixed on a plain wall, and that a small hole sorts it. Another unit explains how a small hole makes a picture.

items.p: Why do many older people need more light to read?
opts: Their lenses let less light through, and their pupils get smaller with age
Books were printed smaller long ago
items.why: As we grow old, the lens gets a little cloudy and yellow, and the pupil gets smaller. So less light reaches the retina. Picking 'weaker rays' is the old eye-rays idea.

items.p: Do we see the world as it really is? Two scientists who studied seeing gave different answers.

views.who: Anil Seth, a British scientist who studies the brain, 2021
views.says: What you see is your brain's best guess about what is out there. It checks its guesses against the signals from the eyes.
The light reaching your eyes already carries rich information about the world. As you move around, you pick it up directly. No guessing picture is needed.

items.ask: Which idea fits better with what you found in this unit? Give one piece of evidence. Then give one piece of evidence for the other side.
items.a: A strong answer uses real evidence for each side. For Seth: in the blind spot test, the brain filled in a gap with white that the eye never caught. For Gibson: in the lamps activity, each torch's light arrived on its own spot, carrying real information about where that torch was. It may say both can be partly true.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. There is good evidence that the brain fills in and guesses, and also good evidence that light carries a lot of real information.

items.p: Label the parts of the eye on the drawing: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve.
items.a: Cornea at the very front, iris as the coloured ring, pupil as the hole in the middle, lens just behind it, retina lining the back, optic nerve leaving the back.
items.why: Light passes through these parts in order from front to back, and the optic nerve carries the signal on.
items.art: An unlabelled side view of a cut-open eye with six blank label lines.

experiments.title: The Dark Box: can we see without light?
experiments.context: This is the dark box test. You hide three things in a closed shoebox and look through a small peephole. Then you let in a little light at a time.
experiments.question: Can we see anything when there is no light?
experiments.predict: Before you look, guess. What will you see through the peephole when the lid is shut tight? Which of the three objects will you see first when a little light comes in? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, look through the same peephole every time, from the same place. Change only one thing: how far the lid is open. Count slowly to 5 before you answer each time, because your eyes need a moment to settle.
results_table: Could I tell the ball's colour?

materials.item: a shoebox with a lid (any closed cardboard box works)
scissors, used by a grown-up
a small piece of white paper, a steel spoon and a red ball or red bangle
black insulation tape, and a dark towel or cloth to wrap the box in
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the peephole. Do not put fingers near the scissors.

schedule.what: Make the box, guess what you will see, then open the lid a little at a time and record what appears.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw what you saw at each step: total dark, a crack of light, half open and fully open.

flow.do: 1. Do this in a bright room, by day or with the lights on. 2. A grown-up cuts a round peephole, about as wide as a pencil, in one short end of the shoebox. A small hole is easier to seal with your eye. 3. Put the white paper, the steel spoon and the red ball inside, at the far end. Do this without your child watching. 4. Put the lid on and tape the edges. 5. Wrap the box in a dark towel, leaving only the peephole uncovered, because thin cardboard lets some light through.
flow.say: I've hidden three things inside this box. You're going to be a scientist and find out what you can see in there.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut a small hole in a shoebox. Then close your eyes. The grown-up hides three things inside. The lid goes on tight, and a dark towel goes around the box.
flow.context: This is the first step of the dark box test. You hide three things in a closed box, to find out whether we can see without light.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before looking.
flow.say: When you look through the hole with the lid shut, what do you think you will see? If we let a little light in, what will you see first?
flow.kid: Guess first. What will you see with the lid shut? What will you see first when a little light gets in?

ask.q: What do you think you will see with the lid shut?
good: Maybe a little, if my eyes get used to it.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts one eye right against the peephole, and closes the other eye. 2. They cup a hand around the eye and the hole, to keep out light from the room. 3. They count slowly to 5. 4. They say what they can see. 5. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Press your eye to the hole. Count slowly to five. What can you see?
flow.kid: Put one eye right on the hole. Cup your hand around it. Close the other eye. Count to five. What can you see?
flow.parent: With the box wrapped and the hole covered by your child's eye, your child should see nothing at all. Some children say they see 'black'. That is a good observation. Black is what we see when no light reaches the eye. If your child sees a glow, light is getting in somewhere. Wrap the towel tighter, tape any gap, and look again.

check.q: In the dark box with the lid shut, your eye is open but you see nothing. Why?
options: Your eye needs more time to send out its rays
No light is coming from the things into your eye
The things inside are too small
check.why: We see a thing only when light from it comes into our eyes. Inside a sealed box there is no light, so nothing bounces off the things and nothing comes to your eye. Picking 'send out its rays' is the very old idea that eyes reach out to see. If that were true, you would see in the box. Picking 'too small' misses the point, because you see them easily once the lid is open.

flow.do: 1. Unwrap the towel from one corner and lift that corner of the lid just a crack, about the width of a pencil. 2. Your child looks again and counts to 5. 3. Lift the lid halfway, and look again. 4. Take the lid off, and look again. 5. Each time, write down what they saw and whether they could tell the colour of the ball.
flow.say: Now I'll let in a tiny bit of light. What can you see now? Can you tell what colour the ball is?
flow.kid: A grown-up lifts the lid a crack. Look again. What appears first? Then a bit more light. Then all the way. Can you see the ball's colour yet?
flow.parent: Usually the white paper and the shiny spoon appear first, as pale grey shapes. The ball comes later, and its red colour last. White and shiny objects reflect the most light. The cells in the eye that see colour need more light than the ones that see shapes. If everything appears at once, the crack was too wide. Close the lid and try a thinner crack.

flow.do: Compare what happened with the guesses from the start.
flow.say: Were your guesses right? Which thing showed up first, and why do you think it did?
flow.kid: Were you right? Which thing did you see first? Why do you think it came first?
flow.think: If you sat inside a cave with no light for an hour, would you start to see? Why or why not?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about seeing in the dark? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: we need light to see. What I saw: with the lid shut I saw nothing, but when light came in I saw the paper first. Why: the objects only show when light reflects off them into my eye.

experiments.title: Watch Your Pupils Change
experiments.context: In this test you watch the black circle in the middle of the eye, called the pupil. You measure how big it is in dim light and in bright light.
experiments.question: How does the size of my pupil change in dim light and in bright light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the pupil be bigger or smaller in dim light? Why do you think so? Draw what you think it will look like in dim light and in bright light.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, measure the same eye each time, with the same pupil card. Change only one thing: how bright the room is. Wait one full minute in each light before you measure. Measure three times in each light, because one look can be a fluke.

materials.item: any mirror you can stand close to, such as a hand mirror or the bathroom mirror
a pupil card you draw: a row of black circles 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 mm across, on a strip of paper
a room you can make dim, and a table lamp or a torch
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never shine the lamp or a torch straight into anyone's eyes. Never use the Sun. Point the lamp at the wall beside your face, not at your eyes.

schedule.what: Make the pupil card. Measure the pupil in dim light, room light and lamp light. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each kind of light. Make each bar as tall as the middle pupil size.

flow.do: 1. On a strip of paper, draw a row of filled black circles. Make them 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 mm across, using a ruler. Help your child with the small ones. 2. Write the size under each one. This is the pupil card.
flow.say: We're going to measure your pupil, the black circle in the middle of your eye. This card is our ruler. We'll hold it next to your eye and find the circle that matches.
flow.kid: Draw seven black circles in a row. Make them 2 to 8 mm wide. Write the size under each one. This is your pupil card.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pupil test. You watch the black circle in the middle of your eye in a mirror, and measure it in dim and bright light.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim. Close the curtains and switch off the lights. Leave a door open to a lit room, so you can still see a face. 2. Wait one full minute. 3. Hold the pupil card just under one of your child's eyes and find the circle that matches the pupil. Write the size. Do this three times. 4. Swap, so your child measures your pupil too.
flow.say: Wait one minute for your eyes to settle. Now look straight ahead at the wall. Which circle on the card is the same size as your pupil?
flow.kid: You need a grown-up for this. Sit in the dim room for one minute. Look at the far wall, not at the card. The grown-up holds the card under your eye. They find the circle that matches your pupil. Then you measure theirs.
flow.parent: Look closely, from about a hand's width away. Your child must look at the far wall, because looking at something close makes the pupil smaller. Dark brown eyes make the pupil harder to tell apart from the iris. Turn your child's face a little towards the open door, so some light falls on the eye. If you still cannot see the pupil, take a close photo of the eye and the card together, without flash, and zoom in. In dim light many children's pupils are 6 or 7 mm.

flow.do: 1. Turn on the normal room light and wait one minute. Measure three times. 2. Then switch on the lamp, pointing at the wall right beside your child's face, not into the eye. Wait one minute. Measure three times. 3. Last, your child looks into a mirror in the lamp light. They cover one eye with a hand for 10 seconds. Then they take the hand away and watch that pupil.
flow.say: Now the light is brighter. Keep looking at the far wall while I measure. Then look in the mirror. Cover one eye for ten seconds, take your hand away, and watch that pupil. What happens?
flow.kid: Now the lamp comes on beside your face. Wait a minute. The grown-up measures your pupil three times. Then look in a mirror. Cover one eye with your hand and count to 10. Take your hand away and watch that pupil. What happens?

check.q: When the lamp came on, your pupil got smaller. Why does the eye do this?
options: To let in less light and protect the inside of the eye
Because the pupil is tired
To send out more light
check.why: The pupil is a hole that lets light in. In bright light the iris shrinks it, so that too much light does not dazzle the retina at the back. Picking 'tired' usually means thinking the eye is wearing out. It isn't. It opens again in the dark. Picking 'send out more light' is the old idea that eyes give out light. They don't.

flow.parent: When the hand comes away, the pupil is big for a moment, then shrinks in less than a second. This works even with dark brown eyes, because the change is easy to see in bright light.

flow.do: Help your child find the middle value for each light. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each kind of light.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each kind of light gets one bar. A taller bar means a bigger pupil.
flow.kid: Put your three numbers in order. The middle one is your middle value. Draw one bar for each light. A taller bar means a bigger pupil.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about your pupil? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think your eye does this?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my pupil gets smaller in bright light. What I saw: it was 7 mm in the dim room and 3 mm next to the lamp. Why: the pupil is a hole that lets in light, so it opens wide when there is little light and closes when there is a lot.
flow.think: Why do you think a cat's pupil can open even wider than yours?

experiments.title: Break the Light's Journey
experiments.context: In this test you shine a torch on a toy in a dark room. Then you break the path of light in different places, to find out what seeing needs.
experiments.question: What do we need to see a thing that makes no light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If the torch is shining right on the toy, will you always be able to see it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep the toy, the torch and your chair in the same places. Change only one thing each time: where the light's path is broken.
results_table: Is light landing on the toy?

materials.item: a torch, or a phone torch
a small toy
a big piece of card or a hardback book
a room you can make very dark, at night with the lights off and the curtains closed

experiments.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Shine the torch on a toy. Break the light's path in three different places. Record what you can see.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the toy, the torch and your eye. Draw the light's path with arrows, and mark where you broke it each time.

flow.do: 1. Put the toy on a table in a room you can make very dark. 2. Your child sits facing the toy, about two big steps away. 3. Turn off all the lights.
flow.say: The toy makes no light of its own. Let's find out exactly what we need to see it.
flow.kid: Put a toy on a table. Sit two big steps away, facing it. Turn off the lights. Can you see the toy?
flow.context: This is the first step of the light's journey test. You find out what you need to see a toy, by breaking the light's path in different places.

flow.do: 1. Shine the torch at the ceiling at the far side of the room. 2. Then shine it straight at the toy, from the side. 3. Each time, ask how well your child can see the toy.
flow.say: Now I'm shining the torch at the ceiling. Can you see the toy? Now I'm shining it right on the toy. How about now?
flow.kid: First the torch shines at the ceiling. Can you see the toy? Now it shines on the toy. Better?
flow.parent: With the torch on the ceiling, your child may just see the toy, because light bounces off the ceiling and lands on it. This is a good thing to notice. Light can bounce more than once.

flow.do: 1. Keep the torch shining on the toy. 2. Hold the card between the toy and your child's eyes. 3. Then hold the card between the torch and the toy instead.
flow.say: The torch is still shining on the toy. Now I put the card in front of your eyes. Can you see it? Now the card goes between the torch and the toy.
flow.kid: The torch still shines on the toy. A card goes in front of your eyes. Can you see the toy now? Now the card blocks the torch. What happens?

check.q: The torch is shining on the toy, but a card is in front of your eyes. Why can't you see the toy?
options: The toy has stopped being lit
Light bouncing off the toy can't reach your eyes
Your eyes have stopped working
check.why: The toy is still lit, and your eyes are fine. But the card stops the light that bounces off the toy from reaching your eyes. Seeing needs the whole journey: source, then thing, then eye. Picking 'the toy has stopped being lit' means looking only at the first half of the journey. Picking 'your eyes have stopped working' means thinking eyes see on their own.

flow.do: Turn off the torch, with nothing blocking anything.
flow.say: Last test. No card, but no torch. Can you see the toy?
flow.kid: Last test. The torch goes off. No card. Can you see the toy?

chart.title: Made-up example: a filled-in results table
cols: Is light landing on the toy?
rows: Card in front of my eyes

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the torch, the toy and an eye, with arrows for the light. Then ask what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Draw the light's path with arrows. Which way do the arrows go? Then tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Draw the torch, the toy and your eye. Draw arrows for the light. Then say: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.parent: Look at the arrows. Many children draw an arrow from the eye to the toy. If your child does, ask: 'In the dark room, did your eye send something out? Then why couldn't you see?' A good answer: What I think: to see the toy, light must go from the torch to the toy and then into my eye. What I saw: when the card blocked either part, the toy vanished. Why: the toy makes no light, so it needs to bounce light from the torch into my eye.

activities.title: Catch the Invisible Beam
activities.context: In this activity you shine a torch across a dark room. The beam is almost invisible from the side, until you put a fine mist or a little dust into it.

materials.item: a bright torch, or a phone torch
a spray bottle with water (the kind used for plants or ironing), or a pinch of atta
a room you can make dark, at night with the lights off

activities.safety: Spray the mist away from faces and from anything electric. Wipe the floor afterwards so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Shine a torch across a dark room. Look at the beam from the side. Then spray mist into it.

activities.record: Draw the beam before the mist and after the mist. Draw arrows to show where the light goes to reach your eyes.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Put the torch on a table, shining across the room at a wall. 3. Your child stands to the side of the beam and looks at the air in between, not at the torch.
flow.say: The torch is shining across the room. Look at the air between the torch and the wall. Can you see the light travelling?
flow.kid: The torch shines across the dark room. Stand to the side. Look at the air in between. Can you see the beam?
flow.context: This is the first step of the invisible beam activity. You find out why a torch beam is hard to see from the side.

flow.do: Spray two or three puffs of mist into the air just above the beam, so the drops fall through it. If you have no spray bottle, sprinkle a pinch of atta from your fingers just above the beam.
flow.say: Now watch the air when the mist falls through it.
flow.kid: A grown-up sprays mist, or sprinkles atta, above the beam. Watch the air. What do you see now?

ask.q: Why can you see the beam now?
good: The water drops bounce some light into my eyes.
The mist sends light sideways to me.

check.q: Before the mist, the torch beam was hard to see from the side. Why?
options: The light was going straight to the wall, not into your eyes
Light is too fast to see
The torch was too weak
check.why: We see light only when it comes into our eyes. In clean air the beam travels straight to the wall, and almost none of it turns sideways towards you. Mist drops reflect some light in all directions, and some of it reaches your eyes. Picking 'too fast' is a common idea, but speed is not the problem. Picking 'too weak' doesn't fit, because the spot on the wall is bright.

flow.parent: The beam should light up as a bright stripe where the mist or atta falls through it, and fade again as it settles. If you see nothing, stand closer to the side of the beam and make the room darker.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the beam before and after the mist, with arrows showing where the light goes.
flow.say: Draw what you saw. Then draw arrows. Which way did the light go to reach your eyes?
flow.kid: Draw the beam with no mist, and with mist. Add arrows. How did the light get to your eyes?
flow.think: Sunbeams in a dusty room, or through trees on a misty morning, work the same way. Where else have you seen a beam of light?
flow.parent: A good answer: each drop of mist reflects a little light sideways, into my eyes. Without the drops, the light went straight past me to the wall.

activities.title: Find Your Blind Spot
activities.context: Everyone has a blind spot in each eye, where no light can be caught. In this activity you find yours with a cross and a dot on a card.

materials.item: a white card or paper, about the size of a postcard
a black pen
a 30 cm ruler, or a measuring tape

activities.safety: No safety worries. Take a break if your eye feels tired.

schedule.what: Make the card. Find the blind spot in each eye. Measure how far away the card is when the dot vanishes.

activities.record: Write how far the card was from your eye when the dot vanished, for your right eye and your left eye. Ask a family member to try too.

flow.do: On the card, draw a small cross on the left. Draw a filled dot, about as big as a pea, on the right. Put them about 8 cm apart, on the same line.
flow.say: We're going to find a place in your eye that cannot see at all. Everyone has one. This card will show us.
flow.kid: Draw a small cross on the left of the card. Draw a black dot on the right, 8 cm away. Make them the same height.
flow.context: This is the first step of the blind spot activity. You draw a cross and a dot on a card to find the place in your eye that cannot catch light.

flow.do: 1. Your child covers their left eye with their hand. 2. They hold the card at arm's length and stare at the cross with the right eye. 3. They slowly bring the card closer, still staring at the cross. 4. When the dot disappears, stop. Measure from the eye to the card with the ruler.
flow.say: Keep looking only at the cross. Don't look at the dot. Bring the card slowly closer. Tell me the moment the dot vanishes.
flow.kid: Cover your left eye. Stare at the cross with your right eye. Bring the card slowly closer. Does the dot vanish? Stop there!
flow.parent: With the marks 8 cm apart, the dot usually vanishes when the card is about 25 to 35 cm from the eye. If it doesn't, check your child is staring at the cross, not the dot. For the left eye, cover the right eye and stare at the dot instead. The cross will vanish.

flow.do: Talk about why the dot vanished, and what your child saw in its place.
flow.say: When the dot vanished, what did you see where it had been? A black hole, or plain white card?
flow.kid: When the dot vanished, what was there instead? A hole? Or plain white card?

check.q: When the dot vanished, you saw plain white card, not a hole. Why?
options: Your brain filled in the gap with what is around it
The dot really disappeared from the card
Your eye sent out a ray that rubbed it out
check.why: The dot's light landed on your blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves the eye and there are no light-catching cells. Your brain fills the gap with what is around it, plain white card. Picking 'the dot really disappeared' is easy to check: open both eyes and it is back. Picking 'the eye sent out a ray' is the old eye-rays idea. Eyes do not send anything out.

flow.think: You have a blind spot in each eye all day long, and you never notice it. What else might your brain be filling in?

activities.title: Night Eyes: 20 minutes in the dark
activities.context: In this activity you sit in the dark at night and count stars at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes. You find out how your eyes get used to the dark.

materials.item: a cardboard tube from a roll of kitchen paper or foil, or a sheet of paper rolled into a tube
a torch with red cellophane or a red sweet wrapper taped over the front (red cellophane is sold at stationery shops)
a mat to sit on, and a notebook
a clock or phone with the screen turned down

activities.safety: A grown-up must be with the child on a balcony, terrace or roof at night. Stay well away from the edge.

schedule.what: On a clear evening, go to the darkest place you can reach. Count stars through a tube at 0, 10 and 20 minutes.

activities.record: Write the number of stars you counted through the tube at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. On a clear night, go with your child to the darkest place you can reach, like a balcony or a terrace. 2. Turn off any lights you can. 3. Pick one patch of sky. Look at it through the cardboard tube, and count the stars you see.
flow.say: Look through the tube at this patch of sky. Count every star you can see. We'll count again in a while and see if anything changes.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, go somewhere dark at night. Look at the sky through the tube. Count the stars you see. Write the number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the night eyes activity. You count stars through a tube to find out how your eyes change in the dark.
flow.parent: In a big city you may see only a few stars, or none. Then do it indoors instead. Put 10 small objects, like coins, buttons and a white paper, on the floor of a dark room at night, with only a little light from under the door. Count how many you can see at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Sit quietly for 10 minutes. Do not look at a phone or a white light. If you need to see your notebook, use the red torch. 2. Count the stars in the same patch again. 3. Wait 10 more minutes and count once more.
flow.say: No bright lights now, not even a phone. A bright light would spoil your night eyes. We'll use only the red torch. Let's count again.
flow.kid: Sit still for 10 minutes. No phone, no bright light. Use only the red torch. Then count the stars again. Wait 10 more minutes. Count again.
flow.parent: Most people count more stars at 10 minutes and even more at 20. The pupils open wide in a few seconds, but the bigger change is the rod cells building up their light-catching chemical. Rod cells hardly respond to red light, so a dim red torch does not undo their work. While you wait, tell your child about Ibn al-Haytham, or play a quiet guessing game about night sounds.

flow.do: Back inside, help your child draw a bar chart of the three counts. Then ask what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's make a bar for each count. What happened to the number of stars? The sky didn't change, so what did?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each count. Did the number go up? The sky stayed the same. So what changed?

check.q: You counted more stars after 20 minutes in the dark. What changed?
options: More stars came out
Your eyes became more sensitive to dim light
Your eyes started making their own light
check.why: The stars were there all along. In the dark, your pupils opened wide and your rod cells slowly got much better at catching faint light. So dim stars that were too faint at first became visible. Picking 'more stars came out' is a natural guess, but the sky barely changes in 20 minutes. Picking 'eyes making their own light' mixes up eyes with light sources. Eyes only catch light.

activities.title: Ibn al-Haytham's Lamps
activities.context: About a thousand years ago, Ibn al-Haytham put lamps outside a small hole into a dark room. In this activity you do the same with torches and a shoebox.

materials.item: a shoebox
aluminium foil and tape
tracing paper or baking paper, or a sheet of thin white paper
a pin or a sharp pencil, used by a grown-up
3 torches, or 3 phones with their torches on (2 are enough if that is all you have)
a dark cloth or towel

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes. Never shine the torches into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Make the box. Shine three torches at the pinhole. Cover one torch at a time and watch its spot.

activities.record: Draw the three spots on the screen. Then draw what happened when you covered each torch.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a square hole, about 3 cm wide, in one short end of the shoebox, and tapes foil over it. 2. They make one small hole in the foil with a pin or pencil tip. 3. Cut away the other short end and tape tracing paper over it. This is the screen.
flow.say: We're going to make a little dark room, like Ibn al-Haytham's. Light can only get in through one tiny hole.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a small hole in foil on the box. Tape tracing paper over the other end. That is your screen.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ibn al-Haytham's lamps. You make a dark box with one small hole, to find out where light goes.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Stand three torches in a row on a table, about one hand apart, all pointing at the pinhole. 3. Put the box about half a metre away. 4. Your child looks at the tracing-paper screen, with the dark cloth over their head and the end of the box.
flow.say: Look at the screen. How many spots of light can you see?
flow.kid: Turn on three torches in a row. Point them at the hole. Put the cloth over your head. Look at the screen. How many spots?
flow.parent: You should see three small spots of light on the screen, one for each torch. Notice that the order is swapped. The left torch makes the right spot. That is because light travels in straight lines through the hole, which another unit explains. Today we only need this: each torch makes its own spot. If the spots are too faint, make the pinhole a little bigger, or move the torches closer.

flow.do: Cover one torch with your hand. Your child watches the screen and says which spot vanished. Then try the other torches.
flow.say: I'm covering one torch now. What happened on the screen?
flow.kid: A grown-up covers one torch. Watch the screen. What happened? Try each torch.

check.q: When one torch was covered, only one spot went out. What does that show?
options: Each torch's light travels from the torch into the box
The box makes the light itself
Your eye sends out three rays
check.why: Each spot is made by light that travelled from one torch, through the hole, to the screen. Block that torch and its light never arrives. Ibn al-Haytham used this to show light goes from things to where it lands, not the other way. Picking 'the box makes the light' doesn't fit, because the spots go out when the torches do. Picking 'your eye sends out rays' doesn't fit either. Your eye did not change, but a spot vanished.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Like Ibn al-Haytham, tell me: what do you think now about where light goes? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: light goes from each torch into the box. What I saw: when one torch was covered, only its spot vanished. Why: each torch sends its own light, and blocking it stops that light arriving. Your eye works the same way: it is a dark room with a small hole, the pupil.
flow.think: Your eye is a small dark room with a hole at the front. What is the 'screen' inside your eye called?

activities.title: Eyeshine and Red Eyes
activities.context: In this activity you look for glowing eyes at night, and red eyes in flash photos. You find out that the glow is light reflected back, not light made by the eye.

materials.item: a torch
a phone camera with a flash

activities.safety: A grown-up comes on the evening walk. Stay far from street dogs and never disturb an animal. Never shine a torch into a person's eyes.

schedule.what: On an evening walk, look for eyeshine with a torch held next to your eyes. At home, take a flash photo in dim light and look for red eyes.

activities.record: Draw an animal with eyeshine. Draw an arrow from the torch to the eye, and an arrow bouncing back to you.

flow.do: 1. On an evening walk, hold the torch right beside your own eyes, pointing ahead. 2. Look for a pair of glowing dots in the dark, from a cat, a dog or a cow. 3. Stay far away from the animal and keep walking calmly.
flow.say: Hold the torch right next to your eyes. If an animal's eyes are out there, they will flash back at us. Do the eyes glow when we turn the torch off?
flow.kid: Go on an evening walk with a grown-up. Hold the torch next to your eyes. Look for glowing eyes. Turn the torch off. Do they still glow?
flow.context: This is the first step of the eyeshine activity. You look for animal eyes that seem to glow at night, to find out where the glow comes from.

flow.do: 1. At home, dim the room. 2. Take a flash photo of a family member looking straight at the phone. 3. Look at their eyes in the photo.
flow.say: Look at the eyes in the photo. Are they red? The flash went in through the pupil and reflected off the back of the eye.
flow.kid: Take a flash photo of someone in a dim room. Look at their eyes. Are they red?
flow.parent: Many phones now remove red eye by themselves, so you may need a few tries, or an older phone. If you see no animal on the walk, that is fine: the photo works at home. Red eye happens because the back of the eye, behind the retina, is full of tiny blood vessels. The flash reflects off it, straight back to the camera.

flow.do: Ask what the glowing eyes and the red eyes have in common.
flow.say: When you turned off the torch, did the eyes still glow? So were they making light, or bouncing it?
flow.kid: Did the eyes glow with the torch off? So do eyes make light, or bounce it?

check.q: A cat's eyes glow in your torch beam. Where does the glow come from?
options: The cat's eyes make their own light
Your torch's light bounces off a shiny layer at the back of the cat's eye
The cat is sending out rays to see you
check.why: Cats have a shiny layer behind the retina. It bounces light back through the retina for a second chance to be caught, which helps cats see in dim light. Some of that light comes back out to you. Turn off the torch, and the glow stops. Picking 'makes its own light' is very common, but cats' eyes are not light sources. Picking 'sending out rays' is the old eye-rays idea.

activities.title: Draw How You See
activities.context: In this activity you draw a picture of how you see a thing, with arrows. You draw it at the start of the unit and again at the end, and compare.

materials.item: paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw how you see a ball, before learning about it. Draw it again at the end of the unit, and compare.

activities.record: Keep both drawings side by side. Write one sentence on what changed.

flow.do: Before teaching anything, ask your child to draw themselves looking at a ball, with a lamp in the room. Ask them to add arrows to show how they see the ball.
flow.say: Draw yourself looking at a ball. There's a lamp in the room too. Now add arrows to show how you see the ball. There's no right or wrong yet.
flow.kid: Draw yourself looking at a ball. Draw a lamp too. Add arrows to show how you see the ball.
flow.parent: Do not correct the drawing. Many children draw an arrow from their eye to the ball, or no arrows at all. Both are the ideas people had for thousands of years. Keep the drawing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the drawing activity. You draw how you think you see a ball, before you learn about it.

flow.do: At the end of the unit, ask your child to draw the same picture again, without looking at the first one.
flow.say: Draw the same picture again: you, a ball and a lamp. Add arrows to show how you see the ball.
flow.kid: Draw it again: you, a ball and a lamp. Add arrows. How do you see the ball?

check.q: Which drawing shows how you see a ball in a lit room?
options: An arrow from the lamp to the ball, and from the ball to the eye
An arrow from the eye to the ball
An arrow from the lamp to the eye only
check.why: Light goes from the lamp to the ball. It bounces off the ball and travels into your eye. Picking 'eye to ball' is the old eye-rays idea. Picking 'lamp to eye only' explains how you see the lamp, but not the ball.

flow.do: Put both drawings side by side and talk about what changed.
flow.say: Look at both drawings. What's different? What made you change your mind?
flow.kid: Put your two drawings side by side. What changed? What made you change your mind?
flow.think: Scientists change their drawings when they find new evidence. What was your evidence?

projects.title: Eye in a Box
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a model eye from a shoebox. It has a pupil you can make bigger or smaller, and a paper retina at the back where the light lands.

materials.item: a shoebox
aluminium foil, tape and glue
tracing paper or baking paper, or a sheet of thin white paper
a strip of stiff card, about 4 cm by 20 cm, for the iris slider
a pencil, a pin and scissors, used by a grown-up
a piece of wool or string, for the optic nerve
a table lamp
paints or crayons, to colour the iris

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Never look at the Sun through the box or any hole.

schedule.what: Build the box eye: the cornea window, the iris slider with three pupil sizes, and the retina screen. Paint the iris.
Test the eye in a dark room with a lamp. Try each pupil size. Label the parts and show the family how it works.

projects.record: Draw what you saw on the retina screen with the small, middle and big pupil. Label the parts of your box eye.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a 3 cm square window in one short end of the box. Leave it open, or tape a piece of clear plastic from a packet over it. This is the cornea. 2. Cut away the other short end and tape tracing paper over it. This is the retina screen. 3. Cut two slits above and below the front window, so the card strip can slide across it.
flow.say: We're building an eye. The front window is the cornea. The paper at the back is the retina, where the light lands.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a window in the front of the box. Tape tracing paper over the back. That is the retina. Cut slits so a card strip can slide across the front.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eye in a Box project. You build a model eye from a shoebox, with a pupil and a retina.

flow.do: 1. On the card strip, a grown-up makes three round holes. Make one as small as a pin, one as big as a pea, and one as big as a coin. 2. Your child paints a coloured ring around each hole. This is the iris. 3. Slide the strip into the slits. 4. Tape the string to the back of the box and lead it to a drawing of a brain. This is the optic nerve.
flow.say: These three holes are pupils of different sizes. The coloured ring around each is the iris. The string is the optic nerve, which carries signals to the brain.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes three holes in the card: tiny, middle, big. Paint a coloured ring around each one. That is the iris. Slide it in. Tape on a string to a brain drawing.

flow.wait: Leave the paint to dry until tomorrow.
flow.do: 1. On day 2, make the room dark and switch on a lamp at one end. 2. Your child holds the box with the front pointing at the lamp, and looks at the retina screen. 3. Slide the strip to try each pupil size. Draw what you see each time.
flow.say: Try the tiny pupil first. What's on the retina? Now the big pupil. What's different?
flow.kid: Point the front of the box at the lamp. Look at the screen at the back. Try the tiny hole, then the middle, then the big one. What changes?
flow.parent: With the tiny hole, your child may see a dim but sharp glowing picture of the lamp. With the big hole, it is brighter but blurry. A real eye has a lens behind the pupil, which keeps the picture sharp even when the pupil is big. Another unit explains how lenses work.

check.q: In your box eye, which pupil lets the most light land on the retina?
options: The big hole
The tiny hole
They all let in the same amount
check.why: A bigger hole lets more light through, so the retina screen glows brighter. That is why your real pupil opens wide in the dark. Picking 'the tiny hole' may come from noticing its picture looks sharper. Sharp is not the same as bright. Picking 'the same amount' misses how much brighter the big hole makes the screen.

flow.do: Help your child label the box eye: cornea, iris, pupil, retina and optic nerve. Then they show it to the family and explain how we see.
flow.say: Now you're the teacher. Show the family your eye and tell them how light gets in and where it lands.
flow.kid: Label the parts. Then show your family. Tell them how light gets into the eye, and where it lands.
flow.think: Your box eye catches light, but it sends no signals on. What does a real eye have that the box doesn't?

challenges.title: Light the Reading Corner Without a Bulb
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must make a dim corner of your home bright enough to read in, using only daylight bounced from a window.
challenges.problem: One corner of your home is too dark to read in during the day. Make it bright enough to read a reading card, using only daylight that comes in through a window. You cannot switch on any lamp.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
Test with the same reading card each time, from the same chair.
materials: a reading card: a sheet with 6 lines of writing, each line smaller than the one above
white chart paper or a white bedsheet
cardboard, tape and books to prop things up
general: Hang a white sheet or white chart paper where the window light hits it. White things bounce a lot of light in every direction, some into the dark corner.
Cover the walls near the corner with white or pale paper or cloth. Dark walls absorb most of the light that lands on them. Pale walls reflect it on.
Open the curtains fully, and move anything that blocks the window.
creative: Prop a sheet of foil or a steel plate to bounce a patch of sunlight onto the white ceiling above the corner. The ceiling then spreads it around.
In some towns, people have made solar bottle lights: a clear plastic bottle of water fixed through a hole in a tin roof. The water spreads daylight down into the dark room below.
Use several white boards in a chain, each one bouncing light a bit further round the corner.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to bring light into the corner. Draw it, build it and test it with the reading card. How many lines can you read now?

flow.do: 1. Make a reading card with 6 lines of writing, each line smaller than the one above. 2. Sit in the dark corner and count how many lines your child can read.
flow.say: First, let's measure. How many lines can you read in this corner right now?
flow.kid: Make a card with 6 lines of writing, big to small. Sit in the dark corner. How many lines can you read?
flow.context: This is the first step of the reading corner challenge. You measure how dark the corner is before you try to bring in daylight.

flow.do: 1. Try one idea at a time, like a white sheet near the window or foil bouncing light onto the ceiling. 2. After each idea, count the lines your child can read. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time, so we know which one helps. After each one, read the card again.
flow.kid: Try one idea. Read the card again. How many lines now? Write it down. Then try the next idea.
flow.parent: Changing one thing at a time makes it a fair test. White and pale things usually help a lot, because they bounce light in every direction. Shiny foil helps only if it is aimed carefully. Never aim bounced sunlight into anyone's eyes.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why the best idea worked, using the words 'reflect' and 'eye'.
flow.say: Which idea worked best? Tell me the path the light took, from the window all the way into your eyes.
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? Say the path the light took. Start at the window and end in your eyes.

check.q: A white sheet near the window made the corner brighter. Why?
options: The white sheet makes its own light
Daylight bounces off the white sheet in every direction, some of it into the corner
The white sheet keeps the dark away
check.why: White things bounce back most of the light that lands on them, spraying it in every direction. Some of that light lands on the reading card and then bounces into your eyes. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes up a lit object with a light source. Picking 'keeps the dark away' treats darkness as a thing. Darkness is only missing light.

challenges.title: A Night Path for Paati
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must help a grandparent find the way from bed to the bathroom at night, without a bright light that wakes everyone up.
challenges.problem: Paati gets up at night to go to the bathroom. When the light is switched on, everyone wakes up, and her eyes are dazzled. With the light off, she cannot see the step or the door. Design a way for her to see the path safely.
constraints: It must not wake people sleeping in the room.
It must not dazzle Paati's eyes when she has been asleep.
Use things that are safe, cheap and easy to find.
materials: card, scissors and a torch for testing
general: Put a small dim night-light low down near the floor. A dim light keeps her night eyes working, and does not dazzle.
Stick white tape along the edge of the step and around the door frame. Pale things bounce the most of what little light there is, so they show up first in the dark.
Clear the path of things she could trip on.
creative: Use a dim red or orange night-light. Our night eyes are less disturbed by red light, which is why astronomers use red torches.
A light that switches on by itself when someone walks past, then turns off again.
Glow-in-the-dark stickers along the wall, at hand height, like a trail of stars.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own night path. Draw a map of the room with your ideas on it. Test it at night with a grown-up. Can someone walk the path with only your design to see by?

flow.do: 1. At night, with the lights off, stand at Paati's bed with your child. 2. Wait a minute. 3. Ask what they can see along the path, and what they can't.
flow.say: Let's see the room the way Paati sees it at night. What can you see? What's invisible?
flow.kid: At night, stand by the bed with a grown-up. Turn the lights off. Wait a minute. What can you see? What can't you see?
flow.context: This is the first step of the night path challenge. You find out what a grandparent can and cannot see when walking at night.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a map of the room and marks their ideas. 2. Try one idea at a time, like white tape on the step. 3. Check it again in the dark.
flow.say: Draw the room and mark your ideas. Then let's try them one at a time and see which ones work.
flow.kid: Draw a map of the room. Mark your ideas. Try one at a time in the dark. Which one helps most?
flow.parent: Remind your child of the dark box test. The white paper showed up first in dim light. The same is true of white tape on a step. Older people often need more light to see than children do, because their lenses let less light through.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why their best idea works, using what they know about light and eyes.
flow.say: Why does your idea work? Tell me what the light does, and what Paati's eyes do.
flow.kid: Why does your idea work? Say what the light does. Say what Paati's eyes do.

check.why: In dim light, pale things bounce back the most light, so they reach our eyes first. That is why the white paper showed up first in the dark box. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes up a lit object with a light source, like a night-light. Picking 'helps eyes send out rays' is the old eye-rays idea.

quiz.p: Nithya sits in a dark cinema hall. The film ends and the screen goes black. She cannot see her friend in the next seat. Why not?
opts: No light is bouncing off her friend into her eyes
quiz.why: Her friend is still there, and Nithya's eyes are fine. But with the screen dark, no light lands on her friend, so none bounces into Nithya's eyes. Picking 'her eyes stopped working' forgets that eyes need light to catch.

quiz.p: Which of these is a light source?
quiz.why: A firefly makes their own light. A steel tumbler only shines because light bounces off it. The full Moon is a rock lit by the Sun. Picking the Moon is very common, because it looks so bright.

quiz.p: A white wall looks bright on a sunny afternoon. Why?
opts: It bounces a lot of sunlight into our eyes
quiz.why: A white wall is a lit object. It bounces back most of the light that lands on it. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes up a lit object and a light source.

quiz.p: Which arrows show how you see a tree in sunshine?
quiz.why: Sunlight lands on the tree, bounces off, and goes into the eye. An arrow from the eye to the tree is the old eye-rays idea.

quiz.p: A doctor shines a small torch into your eye, and your pupil gets smaller. Which part of your eye made the pupil smaller?
opts: The iris, the coloured ring around the pupil
The retina, at the back of the eye
quiz.why: The iris is a ring of muscle around the pupil. In bright light it closes the pupil, so less light gets in. The retina catches the light, and the optic nerve carries the signals to the brain.

quiz.p: What happens to your pupils when you walk out into bright sunshine?
quiz.why: In bright light the iris shrinks the pupil, so less light gets in. In dim light it opens wide. The colour of the iris does not change.

quiz.p: In the pupil test, why did we measure three times in each light?
opts: Because one look can be a fluke
Because the pupil needs three tries to work
quiz.why: Doing a test more than once makes the result more trustworthy. One look might be a mistake. The pupil works every time, but our measuring might not.

quiz.p: In the dark box test, you opened the lid a little more each time. What were you changing on purpose?
opts: How much light got into the box
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing on purpose and keeps the rest the same. Here only the light changed, so any change in what you saw came from the light.

quiz.p: Looking at a very bright light hurts, and leaves a dark blob floating in your sight. What does this clue tell us?
opts: Something came into the eye from the light
The eye sent out too many rays
The blob is a ray stuck in the eye
quiz.why: The eye was pressed on by strong light coming in. Ibn al-Haytham used this clue to show that seeing is light coming in, not rays going out.

quiz.p: Who showed, about a thousand years ago in Cairo, that light comes into the eye?
quiz.why: Ibn al-Haytham wrote the Book of Optics in Cairo. Isaac Newton was born more than 600 years later. Aristotle lived about 1,300 years earlier. He thought something passes from things to the eye, but he did not test it the way Ibn al-Haytham did.

quiz.p: Every eye has a blind spot. Why don't you notice yours every day?
opts: Your brain fills in the gap, and each eye covers the other eye's blind spot
The blind spot only appears in the dark
The blind spot moves about too fast to notice
quiz.why: The blind spot is where the nerve leaves the eye. The brain fills it with what is around it. With both eyes open, each one sees what the other misses.
Light comes in tiny packets called photons. A rod cell in the retina can respond to a single one.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know?
opts: Exactly how the brain turns signals from the eyes into what we experience
quiz.why: Light entering the eye and the pupil changing size are well tested. How the brain turns signals into experience is one of the biggest open questions.

applications: Eye doctors look through the pupil at the retina with a bright light, to check that eyes are healthy.

Cataract surgery replaces a cloudy lens with a clear one. Aravind Eye Hospital in Madurai, started in 1976 by Dr G. Venkataswamy with his sister Dr G. Natchiar and others, has done millions of these operations, many of them free.
An old Indian medical book, the Sushruta Samhita, describes an early operation to push a cloudy lens out of the way.
Cameras, including phone cameras, work by letting light in through a hole and catching it at the back, like an eye.
Night drivers rely on headlights bouncing light off the road, animals and signs into their eyes.
Pale or white paint on walls and ceilings makes rooms brighter, because it bounces more light around.
Astronomers use dim red torches to protect their night eyes.
Safety stripes on steps, kerbs and speed breakers are painted white or yellow, so they bounce enough light to be seen at dusk.
Doctors check the pupils with a small torch after a head injury, because pupils should shrink in light.
Sunglasses and caps protect the eyes by cutting down the light that comes in.
Eye tests at school use a chart of letters getting smaller, to find out how sharply each child sees.
Project Prakash in India helps children born with treatable blindness to see, and studies how the brain learns to see.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn signals from the eyes into the experience of seeing?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know which parts of the brain are busy when we see. But nobody knows how those signals become the feeling of seeing a red mango. Some call this 'the hard problem'.

open_questions.q: Can a person notice just one single photon?
open_questions.why_open: One study in 2016 said yes, sometimes. The result was small, and other teams need to repeat it.

open_questions.q: Do other animals experience seeing the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what a bee's or an octopus's eyes respond to. We cannot get inside their experience.

open_questions.q: Exactly how many times did eyes appear separately in the history of life?
open_questions.why_open: Many scientists think eyes appeared dozens of times. But some of the genes for building eyes are shared by very different animals, so the history is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Why do most people sometimes see faces in clouds and in the fronts of cars?
open_questions.why_open: The brain is quick to find faces. Scientists are still working out exactly how and why it does this so readily.

open_questions.q: How do children who gain sight late learn to see so quickly?
open_questions.why_open: Project Prakash found many learn faster than expected. Exactly how the brain does this is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the pupil test, a child's pupil was 7 mm in the dim room and 3 mm next to the lamp. How many millimetres smaller did it get?
maths.explain: The pupil started at 7 mm in dim light. Next to the lamp it was 3 mm. 7 take away 3 is 4. So it shrank by 4 mm. You can check: 3 + 4 = 7.
maths.context: This is about the pupil test. You measured the black circle in the middle of your eye, called the pupil, in dim light and in bright light, using a card of black circles.

chart.title: Pupil size in two kinds of light

maths.why_maths: Saying 'it got smaller' is a start. Taking away tells us exactly how much smaller, so we can compare with other people's eyes.

maths.problem: In the pupil test, a child measured three times in the dim room: 6 mm, 7 mm and 7 mm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order: 6, 7, 7. The middle one is the second number, which is 7. So the middle value is 7 mm.
maths.context: In the pupil test, you measure your pupil three times in each light, because one look can be a fluke. Then you choose one number to stand for all three.
maths.why_maths: Three measurements are more trustworthy than one. Putting them in order and taking the middle one gives a fair single answer.

maths.problem: In the night eyes activity, a child counted 3 stars at the start, 7 after 10 minutes and 11 after 20 minutes. How many more stars could they see after 20 minutes than at the start?
maths.explain: At the start they saw 3 stars. After 20 minutes they saw 11. 11 take away 3 is 8. So they could see 8 more stars. The sky did not change. Their eyes did.
maths.context: This is about the night eyes activity. You sat in the dark and counted stars through a cardboard tube at the start, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes.
maths.why_maths: The bar chart shows the counts going up. Subtracting tells us exactly how much better the child's night eyes got.

maths.problem: In the blind spot activity, the dot vanished when the card was 25 cm from the eye. Read the ruler in the picture. Is the card nearer or further than a 30 cm ruler's length?
maths.explain: The card was 25 cm away. A whole ruler is 30 cm. 25 is less than 30, so the card was nearer. 30 take away 25 is 5. So it was 5 cm nearer than a ruler's length.
maths.context: This is about the blind spot activity. You drew a cross and a dot on a card, covered one eye, and moved the card closer until the dot vanished. Then you measured from your eye to the card.

chart.title: A 30 cm ruler from the eye to the card
chart.label: Each small mark is 1 cm.

maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres lets you compare your blind spot distance with your family's, and check whether everyone's is about the same.

maths.problem: In the dark box test, 0 of the 3 things were seen with the lid shut, 2 with a crack open and 3 with the lid off. What fraction of the things could be seen with the lid open a crack?
maths.explain: There were 3 things in the box. With the lid open a crack, 2 of them could be seen. So 2 out of 3 were seen. We write this as two thirds.
maths.context: This is about the dark box test. You hid three things in a shoebox and looked through a peephole, letting in a little light at a time.

chart.title: Things seen in the dark box (out of 3)

maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of the whole group we could see. It turns 'some of them' into an exact answer.

roots.context: We have been learning how we see: light bounces off things and comes into our eyes. Now we ask what seeing tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Each eye has one spot with no light-catching cells, where the nerve leaves the eye. In the blind-spot test, the dot vanished when its light fell there, but you saw no hole. The card's white filled the gap. So part of what you see is filled in by your brain.
deep_truth.habit: It questions the habit of thinking our eyes show us exactly what is there, like a photo. The brain builds the picture from the eye's signals, and fills in gaps without telling us.
deep_truth.evidence: In the blind-spot test, with one eye covered, the dot vanished when the card was about 25 cm away, because its light landed on the blind spot. Yet there was no hole: you saw plain white card where the dot had been.

three.who_am_i: You are a light catcher. Light that touched the mango a moment ago is now inside your eye.
three.what_is_life: Many living things, from a money plant on a windowsill to an owl, sense light and live by it.
three.what_is_this_world: Light is always reflecting from object to object, whether anyone is looking or not.

roots.thread: By day, one Sun lights almost everything we see. The mango, the road and your friend's face are all lit by that same light. Each object reflects it in its own way, and that is why they look different. So when you look around, you are catching one light that has touched everything in front of you. This is a small, real picture of oneness: many things, joined by the one light that passes between them and into us.

teachings.teaching: King Janaka asks the sage Yajnavalkya: 'What light does a person live by?' The Sun, says Yajnavalkya. When the Sun has set? The Moon. When the Moon has set? Fire. When the fire has gone out? Speech, a voice to follow. And when all of these are gone? Then the self is the person's own light.
teachings.link: We have learned that eyes see only by light from outside, from the Sun, the Moon or a fire. The sage then asks about a different kind of light: the awareness that knows the seeing, even in the dark.

teachings.teaching: It is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, and the eye of the eye.
teachings.link: The eye catches light, and the brain makes sense of it. But who, or what, is aware of the seeing? The Upanishad points to something behind the eye.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha's teaching, as told by his student Mahakaccana: depending on the eye and on what is seen, eye-consciousness, or seeing, arises. The meeting of the three is called contact.
teachings.link: Seeing is not owned by the eye alone, or by the thing alone. It arises when they meet. Science adds one more thing they need: light. Take the light away, as in the dark box, and seeing does not arise.

science.text: We see only when light from things enters our eyes and lands on the retina, which sends signals to the brain.
How the brain turns those signals into the experience of seeing is not known. Scientists call this an open problem.

other_view.who: Many neuroscientists, and the philosopher Daniel Dennett
other_view.view: Seeing is just the eye and brain processing light. There is no little watcher inside the head, and no need for an 'eye of the eye'. When we understand the brain well enough, there will be nothing left to explain. That is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.title: Let the light come in
practice.say: Let's sit by the window. Close your eyes and take three slow breaths. Now open them very slowly. Don't look at anything in particular. Just let the light come to you. Notice that you don't have to do anything to see. The light from the room comes in by itself. Now close your eyes again. Where did the room go? Open them once more, and let the light back in.
practice.kid: Sit by a window. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Open them very slowly. Don't try to look. Let the light come in to you. Close them again. Open once more.

ask: Light from the mango is inside your eye. Is the mango you see out there, or in here?
If seeing just happens when light comes in, who is the one who sees?
Is the world still there when you close your eyes? How do you know?
When you and a friend look at each other, what are you sharing?
roots.art: A child sitting by a sunny window with eyes gently open, fine threads of light coming from a mango, a tree and a bird outside and flowing softly into the child's eyes.
